photo_spots.description: From the seats behind home plate, the Gateway Arch lines up beyond the outfield walls.

food.name: Broadway BBQ
food.description: St. Louis-style smoked pulled pork and turkey, plus mesquite-smoked brisket carved to order, on bakery rolls.

food.name: St. Louis Slinger Dog
food.description: A ballpark take on the St. Louis slinger: a jumbo hot dog under hash browns, nacho meat, nacho cheese, and an egg.

food.name: Fried gooey butter cake
food.description: St. Louis's classic gooey butter cake, wrapped in warm funnel cake; it was new in 2026.

mascot.name: Fredbird
mascot.description: A cardinal in the team's uniform who leads cheers, shoots T-shirts into the stands, and is known for beaking fans' heads. Kids can find him in the Family Pavilion from first pitch until the start of the third inning.
mascot.fun_fact: He hatched in April 1979, and the Mascot Hall of Fame inducted him in 2025.

seating.title: Budweiser Terrace
seating.description: A general admission standing area in the right-field upper deck, opened in 2019, with bars, drink rails, and a stage.

seating.title: Ballpark Village rooftops
seating.description: Ballpark Village sells tickets to watch from rooftop decks beyond the left-field wall, such as the Bud Deck on the third floor of the Budweiser Brew House.

seating.title: Bring snacks
seating.description: The Cardinals allow outside food in sealed, soft-sided containers, a help on long, hot St. Louis summer days.

chase_field.tagline: A swimming pool sits beyond the outfield wall, under a retractable roof.
highlights: A swimming pool and hot tub sit beyond the right-center field wall and are rented out as a suite one game at a time. The Cubs' Mark Grace hit the first home run into the pool on May 12, 1998.
When it opened in 1998, it was the first ballpark in the United States with a retractable roof over natural grass; the field switched to artificial turf in 2019.
The air-conditioned park was built for Phoenix's summer heat, and the roof stays closed most of the time, opening on game days only when the weather allows.
Game 7 of the 2001 World Series ended here, when Luis Gonzalez's bloop single off Mariano Rivera won the Diamondbacks the title in only their fourth season.

getting_there.transit: Valley Metro's A Line light rail stops next to the ballpark, at 3rd Street/Jefferson for eastbound trains and 3rd Street/Washington for westbound trains. From Sky Harbor Airport, ride the free PHX Sky Train to the 44th Street/Washington station and transfer to the light rail.
getting_there.parking: Garages and surface lots surround the ballpark in downtown Phoenix, including the Chase Field garage next to the park.
getting_there.area: Downtown Phoenix at 4th Street and Jefferson Street, a block from the Suns' arena, with restaurants such as Pizzeria Bianco within walking distance.

photo_spots.name: The pool in right-center
photo_spots.description: Walk the main concourse to the railing above the pool area in right-center field for a look at the park's most famous feature, even without a pool ticket.

photo_spots.name: Arizona Rotunda
photo_spots.description: The three-story rotunda at the main entrance has a map of Arizona set into the floor and large murals on its walls celebrating the history of sports in Arizona.

food.name: Churro Dog
food.description: A warm cinnamon churro on a donut bun, topped with frozen yogurt, whipped cream, and caramel and chocolate sauces; it debuted in 2015.

food.name: Hungry Hill meatball sub
food.description: Meatball subs, Italian beef, brats, and sausages from a stand that has been a staple since the ballpark opened.

food.name: Sonoran-style dog
food.description: A footlong in the style of the Sonoran hot dog, an Arizona favorite topped with bacon, pinto beans, and pico de gallo.

food.name: Versus Dog
food.description: A footlong hot dog whose toppings change with each visiting opponent.

mascot.name: D. Baxter the Bobcat
mascot.description: A bobcat in Diamondbacks gear who has cheered at home games since 2000, mixing with fans of all ages and making mischief around the park.
mascot.fun_fact: Second baseman Jay Bell's 6-year-old son, Brantley, came up with him: the park, then Bank One Ballpark, was nicknamed the BOB, so why not a BOBcat? He debuted on June 23, 2000.

seating.title: Pool suite
seating.description: Groups can rent the pool area in right-center as a suite for a single game, so book well ahead for a summer date.

seating.title: Check the roof
seating.description: The Diamondbacks post each game's roof status, open or closed, on their Roof Information page and roof hotline.

seating.title: Honeywell Sandlot
seating.description: Families with young kids can head to the Honeywell Sandlot, a play area on the Upper Concourse past Section 332.

coors_field.tagline: A row of purple seats marks exactly one mile above sea level.
highlights: Most seats are dark green, but the 20th row of the upper deck is purple because it sits exactly 5,280 feet, one mile, above sea level.
At about 5,200 feet, the field is by far the highest in the majors, so the outfield was built extra deep and game balls have been stored in a humidor since 2002 to tame the thin, dry air.
Behind the center-field wall, a landscape of native Colorado trees, rocks, a waterfall, and fountains shoots water about 40 feet into the air after every Rockies home run and win.
Blue Moon beer was first brewed here in 1995 at the SandLot, the brewery and restaurant built into the ballpark behind the right-field stands.

getting_there.transit: Denver Union Station, two blocks from the park, is served by RTD light rail and commuter trains, including the A Line commuter train to Denver International Airport. RTD buses also serve downtown.
getting_there.parking: The Rockies' own lots at Park Avenue West and Wazee Street open two and a half hours before games and take cards only. Downtown has more than 46,000 parking spaces, about 18,000 of them within a 15-minute walk.
getting_there.area: Denver's historic Lower Downtown (LoDo) neighborhood at 20th and Blake streets, two blocks from Union Station, with bars and restaurants all around the park.

photo_spots.name: The purple row
photo_spots.description: Climb to row 20 of the upper deck for a photo on the mile-high purple seats, with the Rocky Mountains to the west.

photo_spots.name: Center-field fountains
photo_spots.description: The pine trees, waterfall, and fountains beyond center field make a backdrop, especially when the water shoots up after a Rockies home run.

photo_spots.name: Sunset over the mountains
photo_spots.description: Rockies team photographer Kyle Cooper suggests shooting the sky 10 to 15 minutes after the sun drops behind the mountains.

food.name: Rocky Mountain oysters
food.description: Fried bull calf testicles, a Colorado ranch tradition for adventurous eaters.

food.name: Rockie Dog
food.description: The park's signature foot-long hot dog, usually topped with grilled peppers, onions, and sauerkraut.
food.where: Grille Works stands, concourses throughout the park

food.name: Helton Burger Shack
food.description: Made-to-order burgers, fries, onion rings, and shakes at a stand named for Hall of Famer Todd Helton, who wore number 17 for the Rockies.

mascot.name: Dinger
mascot.description: A purple triceratops who roams the park and dances in the seats behind home plate in the late innings to rally the Rockies.
mascot.fun_fact: He hatched from an egg at Mile High Stadium on April 16, 1994. The Rockies chose a triceratops because fossil fragments were found while Coors Field was being built.

seating.title: The Rockpile
seating.description: The bleachers high in straightaway center field. A limited number of low-cost Rockpile tickets go on sale at the Gate A ticket windows two hours before most games.

seating.title: The Rooftop
seating.description: A two-level standing-room area in the upper right-field deck, open to every ticket holder, with bars and panoramic views of downtown and the Front Range.

seating.title: Batting practice
seating.description: Gates A and E open two hours before game time for batting practice, while the other gates open 90 minutes before.

dodger_stadium.tagline: Baseball's largest ballpark, in the hills of Chavez Ravine since 1962.
highlights: Opened in 1962, Dodger Stadium is MLB's third-oldest park after Fenway and Wrigley, and with room for 56,000 fans it is the largest by capacity.
Wavy roofs top both outfield pavilions, one of the stadium's most distinctive features, and a hexagonal video board sits above each.
In the Centerfield Plaza, bronze statues of Jackie Robinson (unveiled in 2017) and Sandy Koufax (2022) stand side by side; the two Hall of Famers were teammates in Brooklyn.
Retired numbers line the left-field facade in the Ring of Honor, and plaques for each honoree and for the Legends of Dodger Baseball line the pavilion ramps.
Willie Stargell hit the first home run completely out of the stadium in 1969, and only a few players since, including Mike Piazza and Shohei Ohtani, have done it.

getting_there.transit: The free Dodger Stadium Express bus runs from Union Station, served by Metro Rail, Metrolink, and Amtrak, starting two and a half hours before games and using a bus lane on Sunset Boulevard. A second Express route runs from the South Bay, starting at Harbor Gateway Transit Center.
getting_there.parking: Large terraced lots surround the stadium, and the Dodgers encourage buying parking in advance; lot gates open about two and a half hours before first pitch. Tailgating is not allowed, and traffic on the roads up the hill can be heavy.
getting_there.area: Chavez Ravine in Elysian Park, just north of downtown Los Angeles and close to Chinatown. Since March 2026 the playing field has been called UNIQLO Field at Dodger Stadium, while the stadium keeps its name.

photo_spots.name: Robinson and Koufax statues
photo_spots.description: The two bronze statues in the Centerfield Plaza, both by sculptor Branly Cadet, show Robinson sliding into home and Koufax in his high leg kick.

photo_spots.name: Top Deck lantern
photo_spots.description: Behind home plate on the Top Deck, a Japanese stone lantern from 1965, a gift from sports columnist Sotaro Suzuki, sits near views out over Los Angeles.

photo_spots.name: Bats and bobbleheads
photo_spots.description: On the Field Level, a display of game-used bats from Dodgers greats sits by Section 50, and a big bobblehead collection sits by Section 51.

food.name: Dodger Dog
food.description: The famous 10-inch pork hot dog in a steamed bun, sold grilled or steamed; Papa Cantella's of Vernon, California, has made it since 2021.

food.name: Tsukiji Gindaco takoyaki
food.description: Octopus-filled takoyaki balls from a popular Japanese chain; the stand opened in 2024.

food.name: Carne asada
food.description: Carne asada tacos, nachos, and fries, a nod to the city's taqueria culture.
food.where: Hornitos Cantina (outfield plazas) and LA Taqueria (Loge 106, Reserve 17)

seating.title: Pavilions
seating.description: The outfield pavilions sit under the wavy roofs, and since the 2020 renovation, elevators and escalators connect them to the Centerfield Plaza and the other levels.

seating.title: Home Run Seats
seating.description: Added in 2021, these seats sit just beyond the outfield wall in left and right field, in front of the pavilions.

seating.title: Postgame shows
seating.description: After select games, fans can watch the fireworks or drone show from the outfield grass, though space on the field is limited.

seating.title: Bring food
seating.description: Outside food is allowed in a clear bag no larger than 12 by 12 by 6 inches, along with factory-sealed plastic bottles of non-alcoholic drinks up to 1 liter.

petco_park.tagline: The corner of a 1909 brick warehouse serves as the left-field foul pole.
highlights: The 1909 Western Metal Supply building, a city historic landmark, was saved and built into left field, and its southeast corner serves as the foul pole. A ball off the east wall is a home run, and a ball off the south wall is foul.
Gallagher Square, a sloping grass park beyond the outfield that was renovated for the ballpark's 20th anniversary in 2024, lets fans watch from the lawn and opens to the public on some non-game days.
The Padres Hall of Fame, opened in 2016 beyond the left-field seats, covers San Diego baseball back to its Pacific Coast League days, and a statue of Trevor Hoffman stands nearby.
Fireworks and a foghorn go off from the scoreboard when the Padres take the field and after every Padres home run.

getting_there.transit: All three San Diego Trolley lines (Green, UC San Diego Blue, and Orange) serve the ballpark, with the 12th and Imperial station facing the main entrance and the Gaslamp Quarter station about a block away. Coaster commuter trains stop at Santa Fe Depot, where riders can transfer to the Green Line.
getting_there.parking: Downtown parking is limited, so the Padres urge fans to pre-purchase a spot in a Padres lot or take transit, and all Padres lots are cashless. Tailgating is allowed on a limited basis at Tailgate Park.
getting_there.area: The East Village in downtown San Diego, next to the Gaslamp Quarter and across from the Convention Center, with San Diego Bay a few blocks west.

photo_spots.name: Western Metal building corner
photo_spots.description: The yellow line painted on the building's southeast corner marks the left-field foul pole, though the corner itself is what counts.

photo_spots.name: Tony Gwynn statue
photo_spots.description: The Hall of Famer's statue watches over the field from the Tony Gwynn Terrace in Gallagher Square, beyond right field, next to an exhibit on his life.

photo_spots.name: Jerry Coleman statue
photo_spots.description: At the east entrance, the beloved broadcaster is shown in his Marine Corps pilot's uniform, with images from his life on the wall behind him.

photo_spots.name: Home Plate Gate
photo_spots.description: Palm-lined steps lead up to the main entrance at Park Boulevard and Imperial Avenue, under the big Petco Park sign.

food.name: Fish tacos
food.description: San Diego's signature taco, sold at local stands such as Puesto.

food.name: Hodad's burgers
food.description: Burgers from Hodad's, a famed San Diego burger joint.
food.where: Mercado near Section 104, and Sections 131, 230, and 300

food.name: Tri-tip nachos

mascot.name: Swinging Friar
mascot.description: A cheerful, balding friar in a hooded robe, sandals, and a rope belt who swings a baseball bat and roams the park.
mascot.fun_fact: He dates to the Pacific Coast League Padres, before San Diego joined the majors in 1969, and he is named for the Franciscan friars who founded Mission San Diego de Alcala.

seating.title: Sun and shade

oracle_park.tagline: Home runs splash into San Francisco Bay over the right-field wall.
highlights: Beyond the 24-foot brick right-field wall lies McCovey Cove, an arm of San Francisco Bay, where fans in kayaks and boats wait for home run balls.
A counter on the right-field wall tallies Giants splash hits into the Cove, more than 100 since 2000, and Barry Bonds hit 35 of them.
Triples Alley, the deep right-center corner 415 feet from home plate, was designed to recall the Polo Grounds, the Giants' old home in New York.
An 80-foot Coca-Cola bottle with slides and a giant vintage three-finger glove sit in the Fan Lot above the left-field bleachers, which looks out on the bay and the Bay Bridge.
Since 2020, both bullpens have sat behind the center-field wall, on either side of The Garden, a working mini-farm below the bleachers where fans can get food and drinks.

getting_there.transit: Muni Metro's 2nd and King station is right outside the ballpark, and Caltrain's San Francisco station at 4th and King is about a block and a half away. On game days, ferries from Larkspur and the East Bay dock at the landing behind center field.
getting_there.parking: Dozens of lots and garages surround the park, but Giants-controlled lots require a SpotHero reservation bought in advance. Informal tailgating is allowed around your car in Lot A.
getting_there.area: South Beach on the San Francisco waterfront, along China Basin at Third and King streets, about a mile down the Embarcadero from the Ferry Building.

photo_spots.name: Willie Mays statue
photo_spots.description: The 9-foot bronze of the Say Hey Kid stands at the main entrance on Willie Mays Plaza, ringed by 24 palm trees for his number 24.

photo_spots.name: McCovey Point
photo_spots.description: Willie McCovey's statue stands across the Cove at McCovey Point in China Basin Park, with the ballpark's right-field wall across the water.

photo_spots.name: Coca-Cola Fan Lot
photo_spots.description: The giant bottle and glove above the left-field bleachers frame shots of the field and the bay.

food.name: Gilroy Garlic Fries
food.description: Fries tossed with garlic, the iconic Oracle Park dish; you will smell them before you see them.

food.name: Crazy Crab'z sandwich
food.description: Dungeness crab piled between two slices of buttery grilled sourdough, a signature item and fan favorite.

food.name: Orlando's Cha-Cha Bowl
food.description: A Caribbean-style bowl from Orlando's, the stand named for Giants Hall of Famer Orlando Cepeda.

food.name: Ghirardelli hot fudge sundae
food.description: Vanilla ice cream with handmade hot fudge, whipped cream, almonds, and a cherry from San Francisco's Ghirardelli chocolate company.

mascot.name: Lou Seal
mascot.description: A friendly seal in Giants gear who has been a regular at Giants home games since 1996 and makes appearances all over San Francisco.
mascot.fun_fact: His full name is Luigi Francisco Seal, he was born on July 25, 1996, and fans picked his name in a contest; it honors the San Francisco Seals, the city's Pacific Coast League team until 1957. He entered the Mascot Hall of Fame in 2024.

seating.title: Free Viewing Portal
seating.description: Anyone can watch through the right-field fence for free from this first-come, first-served spot on the waterfront, a nod to the old Knothole Gangs. Fans may be rotated out every three innings when it is busy.

seating.title: Arcade
seating.description: A few rows of seats sit right above the brick right-field wall, overlooking McCovey Cove.

seating.title: Bullpen Boardwalk
seating.description: Underneath the bleachers, the Bullpen Boardwalk has free skee-ball, pop-a-shot, cornhole, and other games, with no tickets or tokens needed.
